contract_plain_english: Method 4s3pC is the four-stage additive method with the coefficients printed on page 18 and with no direct F^epsilon contribution in the output because b^epsilon is zero. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list] For well-behaved tau, it has the stated global envelope O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^3); for nonsmooth tau such as chopping, the perturbation term drops to O(epsilon Delta t^2) while the scheme term remains O(Delta t^3). [PDF pp. 6, 18, anchors: chopping discussion and two Method 4s3pC error forms] Figure 6 confirms the separate regimes in the paper's diffusion test: the centered-difference perturbation remains third order, while half-precision chopping starts third order and reduces to second order as Delta t decreases. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchors: Figure 6 caption and interpretation]

source_evidence.observation: The smooth analysis assumes bounded derivatives and permits cancellation; chopping produces a bounded but non-Lipschitz F^epsilon and a tau whose derivatives may not exist.
The simplified perturbation order conditions apply only when tau is well behaved.
Method 4s3pC is introduced specifically as a method satisfying the less restrictive conditions (3.5), unlike the preceding methods designed for nonsmooth tau.

source_evidence.anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list and the two displayed error forms
source_evidence.observation: The paper specifies the four-stage coefficients and states separate global error forms for well-behaved and non-well-behaved tau: O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^3) and O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^2), respectively.

source_evidence.anchor: diffusion-equation test setup and Figure 6 caption
source_evidence.observation: The test evolves u_t = u_xx on (0,2pi) with periodic boundaries and initial data sin(x), using a Fourier spectral F and either a centered-difference or chopped Fourier F^epsilon.

The centered-difference perturbation exhibits the expected third-order perturbation regime; half-precision chopping with epsilon = 10^-4 starts third order and reduces to second order as Delta t decreases.

statement.algorithm_linkage: The contract concerns Method 4s3pC with exactly the coefficient data printed on page 18 and the additive F/F^epsilon stage structure of Eq. (3.1); the smooth and chopped claims are two regimes of this same method, not two merged algorithms. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list and error forms; PDF p. 4, anchor: Eq. (3.1)]
binders: Method 4s3pC is a four-stage additive Runge-Kutta method with coefficient matrices A and A^epsilon and weights b and b^epsilon, acting on F and F^epsilon as in the general additive framework. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list; PDF p. 4, anchor: Eq. (3.1)]

The error regimes bind the step size Delta t, perturbation scale epsilon, and perturbation function tau, with separate cases according to whether tau is well behaved. [PDF p. 18, anchor: two displayed error forms]
The numerical test binds u(x,t) on x in (0,2pi), initial data u(x,0) = sin(x), periodic boundaries, and the diffusion equation u_t = u_xx. [PDF p. 18, anchor: diffusion-equation test setup]
conclusions: The output weights are b = [0.002837446974069, 0.336264433650450, 0.806376720267787, -0.145478600892306] and b^epsilon = [0,0,0,0]. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list]
When tau is well behaved, Method 4s3pC gives Error = O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^3). [PDF p. 18, anchor: first displayed Method 4s3pC error form]
When tau is not well behaved, Method 4s3pC gives Error = O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^2). [PDF p. 18, anchor: second displayed Method 4s3pC error form]

With centered-difference F^epsilon, which the paper identifies as producing a well-behaved tau in this example, Figure 6 exhibits the expected O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^3) behavior. [PDF p. 19, anchor: first Figure 6 interpretation paragraph]

With half-precision chopped Fourier F^epsilon and epsilon = 10^-4, the Method 4s3pC error is initially third order and reduces to second order for smaller Delta t, matching O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^2). [PDF p. 19, anchor: second Figure 6 interpretation paragraph]

Method 4s3pA, included for comparison because it was designed for badly behaved tau, starts at higher than third order in the plotted range and settles to third-order behavior. [PDF p. 19, anchor: comparison with Method 4s3pA]
constants_and_indexing: Method 4s3pC has four stages and uses one-based coefficient indices a_ij and a_ij^epsilon with the decimal constants printed on page 18. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list]
The spatial interval is the open interval (0,2pi), with periodic boundary conditions and initial value sin(x). [PDF p. 18, anchor: diffusion-equation test setup]

The paper gives epsilon = 10^-4 for the chopped half-precision experiment but does not quantify epsilon for the Fourier-versus-centered-difference perturbation. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchors: test setup and Figure 6 interpretation]
The constants hidden by the O-terms and their dependence on the spatial discretization, final time, stability bounds, and epsilon are not stated. [PDF p. 18, anchor: two displayed error forms]
definitions_and_conventions: Method 4s3pC is designed to satisfy the simplified perturbation conditions (3.5), which the paper says apply only when tau is well behaved. [PDF p. 17, anchor: opening of Section 4.3; PDF p. 8, anchor: Section 3.1.2]

In the smooth scenario, the paper characterizes F and F^epsilon as well-behaved functions whose derivatives exist and are bounded, so tau and its derivatives are bounded and cancellation can be used. [PDF p. 6, anchor: smooth-case paragraph]
In the chopped scenario, F^epsilon = Chop(F) is bounded but not Lipschitz, tau is not Lipschitz, and derivatives of tau may not exist. [PDF p. 6, anchor: chopping paragraph]

The Fourier spectral approximation is the high-resolution operator F; the second-order centered-difference approximation is the low-resolution F^epsilon in the smooth comparison. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Figure 6 caption and discretization paragraph]
In the mixed-precision comparison, F is a double-precision Fourier spectral evaluation and F^epsilon is its half-precision chopped evaluation. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Figure 6 caption]
error_notions: Both displayed formulas are global Error envelopes: the first combines third-order scheme and perturbation terms, while the second combines a third-order scheme term with a second-order perturbation term. [PDF p. 18, anchor: two displayed error forms]

For fixed nonzero epsilon, the nonsmooth epsilon Delta t^2 term can dominate the Delta t^3 term as Delta t decreases; this transition is the interpretation given to the chopped Figure 6 curve. [PDF p. 19, anchor: chopped-regime interpretation]

The Figure 6 observations concern numerical error in the diffusion-equation test, but the text and caption do not define the exact reference subtraction or error norm. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchor: Figure 6 caption and interpretation]
exceptional_values: The Method 4s3pC claim states no assumptions about overflow, underflow, subnormals, NaN, infinity, Fourier aliasing exceptions, or failure of an implicit solve. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchors: coefficient/error passage and numerical interpretation]
higher_order_terms: The smooth result suppresses all omitted terms into O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^3), and the nonsmooth result suppresses them into O(Delta t^3) + O(epsilon Delta t^2); no further powers or leading coefficients are displayed. [PDF p. 18, anchor: two displayed error forms]
The Figure 6 transition from apparent third to second order is an asymptotic dominance interpretation, not an additional remainder formula. [PDF p. 19, anchor: chopped-regime interpretation]
hypotheses: For the higher perturbation-order regime, tau must be well behaved: the surrounding analysis assumes the relevant derivatives exist and are bounded so algebraic cancellation conditions (3.5) are valid. [PDF p. 6, anchor: smooth-case paragraph; PDF p. 8, anchor: Section 3.1.2 and Eq. (3.5)]

For a non-well-behaved tau, including the chopping model where tau need not be Lipschitz and its derivatives may not exist, Method 4s3pC does not meet the stricter perturbation regime and the lower perturbation order applies. [PDF p. 6, anchor: chopping paragraph; PDF p. 18, anchor: second displayed error form]

The global-error interpretation inherits the paper's standing stability assumption; for the experiment using different spatial operators, the paper specifically says a careful stability analysis is required. [PDF p. 2, anchor: standing stability qualification; PDF pp. 18-19, anchor: caution surrounding the centered-difference experiment]

The observed smooth-regime curve uses high-resolution Fourier spectral F and a low-resolution second-order centered-difference F^epsilon; the observed chopped regime uses Fourier spectral F and a half-precision chopped Fourier spectral F^epsilon. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Figure 6 caption and discretization paragraph; PDF p. 19, anchor: Figure 6 interpretation]
implicit_context: The listed A coefficients form the strictly lower-triangular high-precision part and the listed A^epsilon coefficients form a lower-triangular perturbed part under the standard convention that unlisted tableau entries are zero; the page lists coefficients rather than printing full matrices. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list]
Because b^epsilon is zero, F^epsilon affects internal stages but is not directly weighted in the final update. [PDF p. 18, anchor: b and b^epsilon coefficient list; PDF p. 4, anchor: Eq. (3.1b)]

The two error forms are global asymptotic envelopes inherited from the framework, not exact equalities and not claims that the error constants agree between the smooth and nonsmooth cases. [PDF p. 18, anchor: two displayed error forms; PDF p. 5, anchor: general global-error display]

The centered-difference experiment is illustrative rather than a general recommendation; the paper warns that coupling two spatial operators is sensitive and requires rigorous stability justification. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchor: caution spanning the page break]
norms: No spatial norm, vector norm, absolute/relative convention, or time-aggregation norm is specified for either theoretical Error or the Figure 6 vertical axis. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchors: displayed error forms and Figure 6]
numerical_model: The smooth numerical perturbation is a change of spatial discretization from Fourier spectral F to second-order centered-difference F^epsilon, not a floating-point rounding perturbation. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Figure 6 caption and test setup]

The nonsmooth numerical perturbation is a half-precision chopping of the Fourier spectral evaluation, with epsilon = 10^-4 in the reported experiment. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchors: Figure 6 caption and chopped-regime interpretation]

No IEEE operation-level model, rounding mode, underflow model, or relative-error formula is stated; chopping is modeled through loss of Lipschitz regularity and the abstract epsilon-scaled perturbation framework. [PDF p. 6, anchor: chopping paragraph; PDF p. 18, anchor: nonsmooth error form]

undebatable_constraints: The well-behaved and non-well-behaved tau regimes must remain separate: their perturbation orders are respectively three and two. [PDF p. 18, anchor: two displayed error forms]
Both regimes retain the third-order scheme term O(Delta t^3). [PDF p. 18, anchor: two displayed error forms]
The exact printed Method 4s3pC coefficients, including a41^epsilon = -2 and b^epsilon = [0,0,0,0], are part of the source claim. [PDF p. 18, anchor: Method 4s3pC coefficient list]

The smooth-regime Figure 6 evidence uses a centered-difference F^epsilon, whereas the nonsmooth order reduction uses half-precision chopping; these numerical variants must not be conflated. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchors: Figure 6 caption and interpretation]

The use of different spatial operators carries an explicit stability warning and is not recommended without rigorous justification. [PDF pp. 18-19, anchor: caution surrounding the centered-difference experiment]
